[[File:Tokyo_Wikivoyage_locator_maps_-_Minato.png|120px|thumb|right|Location of Minato in Tokyo]]
'''Minato''' (港区) is a ward in central [[Tokyo]]. Its name means "port", referring to its seaside location, although many areas in the district are quite far from the sea now due to reclamation.

==Understand==
Minato is a fairly sprawling ward with no single center. It is known as a very wealthy part of Tokyo and home to most of Tokyo's foreign embassies, many of its large multinational corporations and a number of prestigious universities.

The following parts of Minato have their own articles:

* '''[[Tokyo/Akasaka|Akasaka]]''' - a business district and nightlife area near the government center
* '''[[Tokyo/Odaiba|Odaiba]]''' - the Tokyo of the future built on reclaimed land in Tokyo Bay
* '''[[Tokyo/Roppongi|Roppongi]]''' - Tokyo's hub for contemporary art and nightlife
* '''[[Tokyo/Shinbashi|Shinbashi]]''' - an older business and commercial district
* '''[[Tokyo/Shiodome|Shiodome]]''' - a still-growing cluster of brand new skyscrapers

===Tourist Information Site===
[https://visit-minato-city.tokyo/en/ Visit Minato City] is the ward's official multilingual guide site.

===By train===
* '''Hamamatsuchō''' (浜松町), terminus of the Tokyo Monorail from Haneda Airport; the closest station on the Yamanote to Tokyo Tower (10-min walk) and Roppongi (25-min walk).
*'''Daimon''' (大門), By underground station Asakusa line and Oedo line.

===By bus===
* '''Hamamatsuchō Bus Terminal''' (浜松町バスターミナル), Exway buses came from [[Chiba (prefecture)|Chiba]] (ex [[Choshi]], [[Kisarazu]]) and [[Tohoku]] (ex [[Yamagata]], [[Hirosaki]]). '''Closed for re-building, reopen due March 2027.'''

===By boat===
* '''[http://www.tptc.co.jp/en/c_terminal/takeshiba Takeshiba Passenger Ship Terminal]''' (竹芝桟橋, Takeshiba Sanbashi) by boat from [[Izu Islands|Izu]] and [[Ogasawara Islands]].

* {{see

| address= | lat=35.658611 | long=139.745556 | directions=the nearest station is Akabanebashi (5-min walk) although Hamamatsucho and Daimon are accessible through several lines and only slightly farther away

| wikipedia=Tokyo Tower | image=Tokyo Tower 20060211.JPG | wikidata=Q183536
| lastedit=2024-02-09
| content=This was a newly re-industrialized Japan's 1958 answer to [[Paris]]'s Eiffel Tower &mdash; a bit more modern-looking and 9 m taller. Entry to the Main Observatory (150m) is &yen;820, while ascending to the Special Observatory (250m) is an extra &yen;600. Your photo will be taken for purchase later (&yen;600). Tip: To get a good view of, and picture with, the tower, try the courtyard in front of Zojoji (nearby), or the second-floor deck outside the Mori Tower at Roppongi Hills. (Some consider that there are better alternatives for views, including the Tokyo SkyTree tower [[Tokyo/Sumida#See & Do|Sumida ward]] which is twice as high, or the [[Tokyo/Shinjuku|Shinjuku]]'s Metropolitan Government Building observatory instead).
}}
* {{see
| name=Zōjō-ji Temple | alt=増上寺 | url=http://www.zojoji.or.jp/en/index.html | email=
| address=Shibakoen 4-7-35 | lat=35.657479 | long=139.748376 | directions=Toei Mita Line Onarimon station
| phone= | tollfree=
| hours= | price=
| wikipedia=Zōjō-ji | image=Zojoji frontal steps.jpg | wikidata=Q249139
| lastedit=2024-02-09
| content=This grand old temple is the headquarters of the Jōdo-shū sect and houses the graves of 6 of the Tokugawa shoguns, but is a little off the beaten track and is rarely visited by tourists. Particularly beautiful around cherry blossom time. It hosts a variety of religious and non-religious festivals throughout the year.
}}
* {{see
| name=Sengaku-ji | alt=泉岳寺 | url=http://www.sengakuji.or.jp/ | email=info@sengakuji.or.jp
| address=Takanawa 2-11-1 | lat=35.637733 | long=139.736275 | directions=Toei Asakusa Line Sengakuji station exit A2
| phone= | tollfree= | fax=
| hours= | price=
| wikipedia=Sengaku-ji | image=Sengakuji 03.JPG | wikidata=Q3176144
| content=A temple most famous as the resting place of the '''47 Rōnin''', a famous group of ''samurai'' who banded together to avenge their unfairly slain master. Having obtained the head of the offender, they brought it to this very temple and then were condemned to commit ritual suicide, like their master. The story is told in ''Chūshingura'', the best-known of all Kabuki plays. History aside, the temple isn't much to look at, but the small museum has artifacts from the event and after, including wooden statues of all the ronin, the banner that the ronin posted during their raid, original letters, and the receipt that the priests wrote out for the head. The graves are a popular site of pilgrimage to this day.
}}
